newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan leads in U.N. race, which inconclusive.
newsitem.headline: Annan leads in U.N. race, which inconclusive.

text.p: U.N. undersecretary-general Kofi Annan on Tuesday obtained the required votes for the top U.N. post but faced one potential veto, thought to be from France, after unofficial Security Council balloting.

Annan of Ghana, in charge of peacekeeping, led three other African candidates and was the only nominee to receive more than the nine votes needed to be elected U.N. secretary-general. But among the votes against him was a veto-bearing permanent member, not officially identified but believed to be France.

The other three candidates, Amara Essy of Ivory Coast, Hamid Algabid of Niger and Amadou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, each received two negative votes from permanent members, believed to be the United States and Britain.

The Security Council began balloting on Tuesday in an effort to select a new secretary-general to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali by Dec. 31, when his five-year term expires. It was the 15-member body's first vote since the United States vetoed the 74-year old Egyptian on Nov. 19.

The 15-seat council held two rounds of unofficial polls, with its five permanent veto-bearing members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France -- voting with marked ballots in the more important second round. The purpose was to gauge the popularity of each candidate.
Council members are scheduled to resume balloting on Wednesday.

Diplomats said that if France changes its mind on Annan, he could possibly be elected this week. "But for the discouragement of one permanent member, we would have had a new secretary-general," said one council envoy.
However, if the council remains at an impasse, new candidates could emerge from Africa, or even from Asia, the next region due to select a secretary-general.
The body's 10 non-permanent members are: Botswana, Chile, Egypt, Germany, Guinea-Bissau, Honduras, Indonesia, Italy, South Korea and Poland.
According to council sources, the following count emerged on the second round of unofficial voting, in which members can support more than one candidate:
--Kofi Annan - 10 votes in favour, 4 against, 1 of them from a permanent member.
--Amara Essy, the Ivory Coast's foreign minister - 7 votes in favour, 4 against, 2 of them from permanent members.
-- Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference -- 5 votes in favour, 7 against, 2 of them permanent members.

--Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former U.N. special envoy for Burundi who now heads the Washington-based Global Coalition for Africa -- 3 votes in favour, 7 against, 2 of them from permanent members.

Boutros-Ghali, vetoed by the United States in a Nov. 19 official vote in which all the other 14 council members supported him, suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4. He could reactivate it at any time but if he does he is all but certain to encounter another veto by the United States, which insists the United Nations needs new leadership to implement reforms.

The council had earlier decided to give priority to Africans on grounds that if the U.S. veto denies the Egyptian incumbent the second term enjoyed by his predecessors, his successor should be another African.

Council President Paolo Fulci of Italy would not give any details of the voting after the closed-door council meeting ended, saying the balloting was a secret as a vote for a Pope of the Roman Catholic Church.
"In Rome, when the cardinals are locked up in the Sistine Chapel to elect the Pope they are forbidden to say anything outside," he said.
"If a new Pope has not been elected, black smoke comes out of the chimney...The moment the Pope is elected, white smoke comes out of the chimney," he added.
"The smoke coming out of the room tonight is black," he said. "We will try again at 11:30 a.m. (1630 GMT) tomorrow morning."
